note: Dante has a reason for asking. In Canto 6 he asked the glutton Ciacco where to find certain great Florentines of the last generation, Farinata first among them, and was told they lay among the blacker souls further down.

A valley beside Jerusalem where, according to the prophet Joel (3:2), God will gather all nations for the Last Judgment. The souls will take back their bodies there, return to their tombs, and the lids will close forever.

context: He lived three centuries before Christ and so was no Christian heretic. Dante puts him here because the name Epicurean was used in his day for anyone who denied the afterlife.

quote: the soul dies with the body
note: The punishment answers the belief. They said the soul ends in the grave, so their souls live on forever in a grave.
The hope of meeting Farinata. Virgil has read it without being told.
Virgil cut short his questions on the bank of the Acheron, in Canto 3, and Dante has been careful since.
A voice from a tomb, breaking in without warning. The speaker has heard Dante talking and knows a fellow Tuscan by his accent.

quote: Your way of speaking reveals you
note: An echo of the Gospel, where bystanders say to Peter: "Your speech gives you away" (Matthew 26:73).

context: The first thing on the speaker's mind, after all his years in Hell, is his city and what he did to it.
He died in 1264, the year before Dante was born. To Dante's generation he was the great enemy, and also the man who saved the city.

quote: as if he held Hell itself
note: One of the best-known images in the poem. Farinata stands in a burning tomb as if it were beneath his notice. Dante admires the greatness and shows its limit: the man is still all pride and party.
A nobleman's first question, and a partisan's: which side is your family on? Dante's family, the Alighieri, were Guelphs of modest rank.

context: Farinata led the Ghibellines of Florence. Dante's ancestors were Guelphs.

note: The Guelphs were driven out of Florence in 1248, with the help of the emperor Frederick II, and again in 1260 after the battle of Montaperti.
The Guelphs came back in 1251, after the emperor's death, and again in 1266–1267, after the Ghibelline cause was broken at the battle of Benevento. Dante answers the taunt with a sharper one.

quote: your people never mastered that skill
note: The skill of returning from exile. After 1267 the Ghibellines never came back to power in Florence, and the Uberti were shut out of every pardon.

context: He interrupts the quarrel about politics with a father's question. The two men share a tomb and were linked by marriage: Cavalcante's son Guido was married to Farinata's daughter.

quote: by virtue of your high genius
note: Cavalcante assumes the journey is a prize for intellect. If so, his son, as brilliant a poet as Dante and his closest friend, ought to be here too.

quote: I don't come by my own power
note: Dante's correction. Genius did not bring him here. He was sent for and is being led.

context: One of the most argued-over lines in the poem. The Italian can mean that Guido scorned Virgil, or that he scorned the one to whom Virgil is leading Dante: Beatrice, or God. Either way, Guido refused something this journey depends on.

note: Cavalcante had a name in Florence for denying the afterlife, so finding him among the Epicureans, asking after a poet son, is enough to identify him.

The past tense. The father hears in it that his son is dead. He was not: Guido was alive at Easter 1300, when the journey is set. He died that August, of a fever caught in exile, and Dante was one of the city magistrates who had banished him in June.
Dante hesitates because he is puzzled. The damned have foretold the future to him, so how can this one not know whether his own son is alive? Cavalcante takes the silence for a yes.

Dante's word is magnanimo, great-souled, a term of praise from Aristotle's Ethics. Farinata has not so much as turned his head at the grief of the man beside him, and picks up his own sentence where it broke off.
The burning tomb. His party's defeat hurts him more than the fire.

context: Named here as the moon, with which the ancients identified her. Her face is "rekindled" at each new month.

note: A prophecy of Dante's exile. Fifty months from the spring of 1300 comes to the summer of 1304. Dante was banished in 1302, and by mid-1304 the exiles' attempts to win their way back, by treaty and then by arms, had failed. He never saw Florence again.

quote: why is that people so merciless
note: The Florentines. They tore down the Uberti houses and left the family out of every amnesty granted to exiled Ghibellines.

A stream near Siena, by the hill of Montaperti. There, on 4 September 1260, the Ghibellines of Siena and the Florentine exiles under Farinata, with German cavalry sent by King Manfred, slaughtered the army of Guelph Florence.

quote: such prayers are made in our temple
note: A bitter figure of speech for the decrees against the Uberti. Why Dante calls them prayers in a temple is uncertain; the city's councils sometimes met in churches.

After Montaperti the Ghibelline leaders of Tuscany met at Empoli and proposed to level Florence. Farinata alone spoke against it, saying he had fought to return to his city, not to destroy it, and the plan was dropped.

quote: you can see what time will bring
note: The puzzle behind Dante's silence. Ciacco in Canto 6 and now Farinata have told him things to come, yet Cavalcante does not know whether his son is living.
The damned are far-sighted. They make out distant events, but as these draw near the view blurs, and of the present they know only what newcomers tell them.

quote: the door to the future is closed
note: The Last Judgment, when time ends. With no future left to see, the damned will know nothing at all.
Cavalcante, who dropped back into the tomb believing his son dead.

context: The pope's party accused him of believing in no afterlife, and Dante accepts the charge, though he admired him as a ruler and patron of poets.

note: Ottaviano degli Ubaldini, a powerful Tuscan cardinal of the mid-13th century, known in his day simply as "the Cardinal". He favored the Ghibellines, and was reported to have said that if he had a soul, he had lost it for them.
Farinata's prophecy that Dante will soon learn how hard it is to come home from exile.

quote: her whose beautiful eyes see everything
context: Virgil promises that she will explain the dark hints about his future. In the event it is Dante's ancestor Cacciaguida who tells him of his exile, with Beatrice at his side (Paradiso 17).

note: Back to the usual direction, after the unusual turn to the right at the end of Canto 9.
The great pit of lower Hell, which begins with the seventh circle. Its stench will stop the poets at the brink in the next canto.
